result.summary: Pausanias traces the kings of Orchomenus after Eteocles: Phlegyas, Chryses, Minyas and Orchomenus. He describes the fall of the Phlegyans, the Treasury of Minyas, and the exile of Hyettus, the first avenger of adultery.

scenes.title: Phlegyas and his warlike people
scenes.summary: Phlegyas succeeds Eteocles and renames the land and city. His people attack Delphi and are defeated.
scenes.stakes: The Phlegyans risk destruction by attacking the god's temple at Delphi.

scenes.title: Homer on the Phlegyans; their ruin
scenes.summary: Pausanias cites the Iliad on the warlike Phlegyans, then says lightning, earthquakes and plague destroyed them.
scenes.stakes: The Phlegyan people are wiped out by disaster.

scenes.title: Chryses, Minyas and the Treasury
scenes.summary: Chryses and Minyas rule; Minyas builds the first Treasury. Orchomenus then gives the town its name.

scenes.title: Hyettus the exile
scenes.summary: Hyettus flees Argos after killing Molurus and is given land by Orchomenus. The Minyae's fame is such that Neleus marries Chloris.
scenes.stakes: Hyettus, an exile for murder, needs refuge and land.

alias_notes.explanation: Old name of the country and city, renamed after Phlegyas.
Name of the Orchomenians, from Minyas, distinguishing them from Arcadian Orchomenians.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias complains that Greeks admire foreign wonders but neglect the Treasury of Minyas and Tiryns walls.

analysis.text: Royal genealogy and divine descent explain the rise and fall of Orchomenus, with impiety toward Delphi bringing ruin.
Pausanias compares Greek monuments with the Pyramids and notes early law on adultery, showing his interest in local heritage and customs.

legacy.text: The Treasury of Minyas, a Mycenaean tholos tomb near Orchomenos, is a well-known archaeological site.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias quotes the Great Eoiae, a poem attributed to Hesiod that survives only in fragments.

language_notes.text: Andreis was the older name of the land and city; Phlegyantis means 'land of Phlegyas'. The king renamed both after himself.
Quoted from Iliad 13, where Ares and his son Panic (Fear) arm for war; the Ephyri and Phlegyans are named as warlike peoples.
The Treasury of Minyas was a great beehive-shaped building at Orchomenus; the walls of Tiryns were massive 'Cyclopean' stonework. Pausanias admires both.
The Great Eoeae was an ancient poem listing heroines and heroes; it was attributed to Hesiod. Its text survives only in fragments.
Draco gave Athens its first written laws around 621 BC; they were famously harsh, hence the word 'draconian'.
Neleus was father of Nestor. His marriage to Chloris links the Minyae of Orchomenus with the royal house of Pylos.

context_notes.text: Eteocles was an earlier king of Orchomenus in Boeotia; Almus was his ancestor in the local royal line.
Delphi was the shrine of Apollo, and attacking it was a serious act of impiety in Greek eyes.
Pausanias presents natural disasters as the people's ruin, implying divine punishment for their impiety.
A Treasury was a strongroom or building for storing wealth, here the ruler's riches.

literary_notes.text: 'Folly and audacity' sums up the Phlegyans as arrogant and reckless, preparing for their punishment.
The earlier attack on Delphi is followed by destruction from heaven, implying divine retribution for the sacrilege.
Pausanias notes that Greeks marvel at foreign wonders while neglecting equal marvels in their own land.
